As a core component of metabolic syndrome and type 2 diabetes, insulin resistance is considered a primary driver of CVD ( 2 – 4 ). It contributes to endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, and accelerated atherosclerosis through mechanisms such as impaired nitric oxide signaling and enhanced oxidative stress ( 2 – 4 ). Traditional methods for assessing insulin resistance, such as the Homeostatic Model Assessment for Insulin Resistance (HOMA-IR), rely on measurements of fasting insulin levels ( 5 ). However, fasting insulin is not routinely measured in clinical practice. To address this limitation, several novel insulin resistance surrogate indices that do not require insulin measurement have been developed, including the triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index, triglyceride-glucose-body mass index (TyG-BMI) index, and metabolic score for insulin resistance (METS-IR) ( 5 – 7 ). Numerous meta-analyses synthesizing evidence on indices such as TyG and HOMA-IR have demonstrated consistent associations with CVD risk ( 8 – 10 ). Nonetheless, it remains unclear which non-insulin-dependent surrogate index exhibits superior predictive ability for CVD. Moreover, no meta-analysis has yet summarized the association between METS-IR and CVD incidence risk. Individual cohort studies have reported varying effect sizes for METS-IR in predicting composite CVD, coronary artery disease (CAD), and stroke ( 11 , 12 ). However, these studies are often limited by small sample sizes, geographic specificity, or inadequate adjustment for confounding factors such as hypertension and lipid-modifying treatments ( 11 , 12 ). Compared with other non-insulin-dependent surrogate indices such as TyG, METS-IR has shown superior predictive value for visceral obesity, incident diabetes, and metabolic disorders ( 7 ). This advantage has been validated against the gold standard for insulin resistance assessment—the hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp technique ( 7 ). In terms of applicability, METS-IR can be manually calculated using a straightforward formula based on routinely available clinical measurements (fasting blood glucose (FBG), triglycerides (TG), high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C), and BMI), making it practical for everyday clinical use without specialized equipment or analyses, as demonstrated in validation studies across diverse populations ( 7 , 13 – 15 ). In diverse populations, higher METS-IR levels are associated with increased arterial stiffness and subclinical atherosclerosis ( 13 – 15 ). Therefore, a rigorous meta-analysis is warranted to quantify the predictive role of METS-IR in CVD incidence risk. This meta-analysis aims to evaluate the association between baseline METS-IR and the incidence of CVD outcomes (including composite CVD, CAD, and stroke) in adult populations without baseline CVD, as well as to explore the dose-response relationship between this index and those outcomes. Ultimately, these findings will provide evidence-based insights to facilitate the integration of METS-IR into global frameworks for CVD prevention. Methods The protocol was registered with PROSPERO (International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews, https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO ) under registration number CRD420251104293. This meta-analysis was conducted following Preferred Reporting Item for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis 2020 guidelines (PRISMA 2020). ( Supplementary Material: Table S1 ). Literature search Articles published from the inception of the databases up to August 2, 2025, were retrieved from PubMed, EMBASE, The Cochrane Library, and Web of Science using the following title terms: “cardiovascular disease”, “CVD”, “coronary artery disease”, “Coronary Disease”, “CAD”, “CHD”, “stroke”, “Ischemic Attack, Transient”, “Peripheral Arterial Disease”, “METS-IR”, and “Metabolic Score for Insulin Resistance”. The search was conducted by combining MeSH terms and free-text words, with no language restrictions applied. The detailed search strategy is described in Supplementary Material: Table S2 . Study selection This systematic review process followed a two-stage screening approach in line with PRISMA guidelines to ensure comprehensive and reproducible study selection. Two researchers independently conducted the entire process from literature search and selection to data analysis. We used Zotero 7.1-beta.41 + 355c61e6d (64-bit) software (Corporation for Digital Scholarship, Vienna, Virginia, USA) to organize all studies. After automatically and manually removing duplicates, relevant literature was initially screened by examining titles and abstracts. Subsequently, full texts of the preliminarily screened literature were reviewed to determine the final eligible studies. Any discrepancies during this process were resolved by a third reviewer. The inclusion criteria for studies were as follows: (1) being a cohort study published as a full text; (2) including an adult population without CVD at baseline; (3) measuring METS-IR at baseline and reporting specific values; (4) having the primary outcome as a composite outcome of CVD and secondary outcomes as individual CVD events; and (5) reporting hazard ratios (HRs) after adjusting for potential confounding factors. The formula for calculating METS-IR is: ln [(2×FBG (mg/dL)) + TG (mg/dL)] × BMI (kg/m²))/(ln [HDL-C (mg/dL)]) ( 7 ). The composite outcome of CVD was defined as the incidence of CAD, stroke, transient ischemic attack, and peripheral arterial disease. The diagnosis of CAD, stroke, transient ischemic attack, and peripheral arterial disease was consistent with the criteria of the original studies. Studies were excluded if they were reviews, meta-analyses, abstract-only articles, or focused on other outcomes. If there was an overlap in the population between different studies from the same registry or group, only the study with the largest sample size was included. Data extraction and quality assessment Two authors independently extracted relevant information from eligible studies, and any discrepancies were resolved by consensus. The extracted data included: (1) first author’s name, year of publication, and country; (2) characteristics of the study design; (3) participant characteristics, including health status, sample size, age, and gender ratio; (4) METS-IR analysis model; (5) follow-up duration; (6) reported outcomes and outcome validation methods; and (7) confounding factors adjusted for in multivariate analysis. For the included cohort studies, the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) was used to assess the quality and strength of evidence for each outcome. This scale, which ranges from 1 to 9 points, evaluates the quality of cohort studies based on the selection of study groups, comparability between groups, and ascertainment of the outcome of interest ( 16 ). Statistical analysis Hazard ratios (HRs) and their corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were used as the general measure to assess the association between baseline METS-IR and the incidence of CVD, CAD, stroke, transient ischemic attack, or peripheral arterial disease in the adult population. For studies analyzing METS-IR as a categorical variable, the HR for CVD incidence comparing the highest METS-IR level to the lowest was extracted. For studies analyzing METS-IR as a continuous variable, the HR for CVD incidence per 1 standard deviation (SD) increase in METS-IR was extracted. Data on HRs and their standard errors were calculated from 95% CIs or P-values; these were then log-transformed for variance stabilization and distribution standardization ( 17 ). Heterogeneity was evaluated using the I² statistic and Cochran’s Q test ( 18 ); if I² > 50% or P < 0.10, indicating significant heterogeneity, a random-effects model was used to pool HR data. Otherwise, a fixed-effects model was applied ( 19 ). Sensitivity analyses were performed by excluding one individual study at a time to test the stability of the results ( 20 ). If more than 10 studies were included for each outcome, subgroup analyses were conducted stratified by gender, age, and diabetes status ( 19 ). Publication bias was graphically assessed using funnel plots. Additionally, when necessary, Egger’s test (for ≥10 included studies) and the trim-and-fill method were applied to further evaluate publication bias ( 19 , 21 – 23 ). The nonlinear mixed-effects model approach proposed by Jiang et al. was adopted to directly integrate data from all studies. Restricted cubic splines (RCS) were used to capture the nonlinear association between METS-IR and the risk of outcome incidence, while incorporating study-level random effects to account for between-study variation, thereby achieving overall modeling of the dose-response relationship ( 24 ). Meanwhile, second derivative analysis was used to precisely locate the inflection points of the curve ( 25 ). When METS-IR was reported in categorical intervals, for closed intervals, the midpoint of the upper and lower bounds of the interval was taken as the exposure level; for open intervals, the interval length was set to that of the adjacent group, and the midpoint was used as the mean exposure level ( 26 ). Meta-analysis and statistical analyses were performed using R software version 4.5.1 (R Core Team, Vienna, Austria). A P-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results Study selection process This study completed literature screening in accordance with the PRISMA statement ( Figure 1 ). A total of 674 relevant studies were retrieved from databases (PubMed, EMBASE, The Cochrane Library, Web of Science). After removing 256 duplicate records, the remaining 418 studies underwent title and abstract screening, and 388 studies that did not meet the criteria were excluded. Through full-text assessment, additional studies were excluded for the following reasons: failure to report multivariable-adjusted HR (n=14), population overlap (n=4), inclusion of participants with baseline cardiovascular disease (CVD) (n=1), lack of specific METS-IR values (n=1), and being non-cohort studies (n=2). Finally, 8 cohort studies were included in the meta-analysis ( 27 – 34 ). Figure 1 Flowchart of the database search and study identification process according to the PRISMA statement. Baseline characteristics of included studies The 8 included studies ( 27 – 34 ) were published between 2021 and 2025 ( Table 1 ), consisting of 7 prospective cohort studies (PC) ( 27 – 31 , 33 , 34 ) and 1 retrospective cohort study (RC) ( 32 ), originating from China (5 studies) ( 29 – 32 , 34 ), South Korea (2 studies) ( 27 , 33 ), and Iran (1 study) ( 28 ). The total sample size was 437,283 participants, with individual study sizes ranging from 2,031 to 306,680. All participants had no CVD at baseline (among them, Lv,2025 ( 34 ) included hypertensive participants without baseline CVD; Yang,2023 ( 32 ) included hypertensive participants with obstructive sleep apnea but without CVD; Yoon,2021 ( 33 ) included participants without diabetes or CVD). The mean age ranged from 39.4 to 59.57 years, and the male proportion was 42.9% to 71.7% (highest in Wu,2025 ( 31 ); lowest in Wang,2023 ( 29 ). Follow-up durations ranged from 1.98 to 17.9 years (shortest in Lv,2025 ( 34 ); longest in Tamehri,2024 ( 28 ). Primary outcomes included composite CVD, CAD, and stroke. Specifically, there were 317 to 5,820 composite CVD events (5 studies ( 29 – 32 , 34 ); total 9,178 events), 198 to 1,216 CAD events (7 studies ( 27 , 28 , 30 – 34 ); total 4,579 events), and 119 to 4,659 stroke events (5 studies ( 28 , 30 – 32 , 34 ); total 6,891 events). All studies adjusted for confounders such as age, sex, smoking, alcohol consumption, hypertension, diabetes, and lipid profiles; some also adjusted for medication use (e.g., antihypertensives, hypoglycemics), physical indicators (e.g., BMI, waist circumference), and sociodemographic factors (e.g., education, marital status). Discussion Main findings The main findings of this meta-analysis are that higher METS-IR levels are significantly associated with increased risks of composite CVD, CAD, and stroke in adults without baseline CVD. Specifically, the pooled hazard ratios (HRs) for the highest versus lowest METS-IR categories were 1.65 (95% CI: 1.36-2.02) for composite CVD, 1.82 (1.50-2.20) for CAD, and 1.47 (1.19-1.83) for stroke. Dose-response analyses further revealed nonlinear relationships for CAD (P = 0.011; inflection at approximately 38.24), marginal nonlinearity for stroke (P = 0.072; inflection at approximately 48.88), and a potential nonlinear pattern for composite CVD (P = 0.145; exploratory inflection at approximately 40.56), beyond which risks accelerate. These results were consistent across categorical and continuous analyses, with moderate-to-high heterogeneity (I²=52.4%-85.6%). Comparison with other studies These findings align with prior meta-analyses on other insulin resistance surrogates, such as HOMA-IR and TyG, which also demonstrate independent predictive value for CVD. For instance, a meta-analysis of 65 studies involving over 500,000 participants without diabetes reported that HOMA-IR was associated with a higher risk of coronary heart disease (HR = 1.46 per SD) compared to glucose (HR = 1.21) or insulin (HR = 1.04) alone ( 35 ). This is similar to our observed HR of 1.18 per SD for METS-IR and CAD. Additionally, a study of HOMA-IR trajectories in 6,755 Koreans showed that increasing patterns over approximately 5 years elevated CVD incidence (HR = 1.59) and mortality (HR = 2.33) ( 36 ), complementing our nonlinear dose-response curves. Compared to TyG, METS-IR’s HR for CAD (1.82) is comparable to reported values [2.01 ( 37 ); 1.94 ( 8 )], though slightly lower, possibly due to our focus on Asian cohorts or differences in adjustments. For composite CVD, METS-IR’s HR (1.65) matches that of TyG-BMI’s [1.62 ( 9 )], indicating equivalent predictive utility despite METS-IR’s simpler components. Biological mechanisms IR, often accompanied by compensatory hyperinsulinemia, serves as an independent risk factor for numerous diseases, including type 2 diabetes, CVD, cellular senescence, tumors, and neurodegenerative disorders ( 2 – 4 , 38 , 39 ). Specifically, in the context of CVD, IR and hyperinsulinemia contribute to vascular and myocardial damage through several interconnected mechanisms. IR impairs endothelial function by reducing nitric oxide bioavailability, promoting oxidative stress, and activating pro-inflammatory pathways such as NF-κB, leading to endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, and accelerated atherosclerosis ( 3 , 4 , 40 ). Hyperinsulinemia exacerbates these effects by stimulating vascular smooth muscle cell proliferation, migration, and extracellular matrix deposition, which fosters plaque formation and vascular stiffness ( 40 ). Additionally, in the myocardium, IR disrupts fatty acid metabolism, inducing lipotoxicity, mitochondrial dysfunction, and increased susceptibility to ischemia, contributing to diabetic cardiomyopathy and heart failure ( 41 – 43 ). These pathophysiological processes form the basis of the association between elevated METS-IR, as a surrogate marker of IR, and the increased incidence of composite CVD, CAD, and stroke observed in our meta-analysis. Observed heterogeneity (I²=52.4%-85.6%) likely stems from study diversity, including baseline characteristics (e.g., hypertension, non-diabetes), follow-up durations (1.98-17.9 years), and geography (e.g., longer follow-up in Tamehri et al. ( 28 )amplifying cumulative effects). The nonlinear patterns suggest threshold effects, where low METS-IR yields gradual risk increases, but exceeding inflections amplifies oxidative stress and lipotoxicity, driving sharper CVD escalation ( 41 – 43 ). Strengths One key strength of this meta-analysis is that it represents the first comprehensive summary of the link between METS-IR and incident CVD. We pooled data from eight high-quality cohort studies (NOS scores: 6-9; total N = 437,283) from China, Korea, and Iran, all of which adjusted for major confounders like age, sex, smoking, hypertension, diabetes, and lipids profiles. Our use of advanced techniques, like restricted cubic splines for dose-response modeling, provides detailed thresholds that could prove useful in clinical settings. The results held up well in sensitivity analyses (with stable HRs) and trim-and-fill adjustments (maintaining significance even after accounting for potential missing studies), despite some heterogeneity. Limitations This meta-analysis, while robust, has several limitations that warrant consideration. First, with only eight studies included, despite the large overall sample size—we could not perform subgroup analyses, as our predefined criteria required at least 10 studies. Second, we detected possible publication bias in the analyses for composite CVD and CAD using trim-and-fill methods, which suggested 2–3 missing studies with null results; while sensitivity tests showed the findings were robust, the actual effect sizes might be slightly smaller (e.g., adjusted HRs: 1.55 [95% CI: 1.28-1.86] for composite CVD; 1.59 [1.32-1.92] for CAD). Third, differences in how METS-IR was categorized, and endpoints were defined (e.g., ICD-10 codes vs. medical records) may have affected the pooled estimates, though we addressed this with random-effects models and sensitivity checks. The moderate-to-high heterogeneity (I²=52.4%-85.6%) across outcomes probably arises from variations in follow-up length, geographic settings, and baseline participant risks; for example, excluding Lv et al. (2025) ( 34 )—which had the shortest follow-up at 1.98 years—sharply lowered I² (e.g., from 85.6% to 0% for composite CVD categorical analysis and 67.9% to 0% for stroke continuous analysis), since shorter studies might miss longer-term effects and increase type II error risk ( 44 ). Fourth, the observational nature of the cohorts limits our ability to infer causality, as unmeasured confounders like genetics could play a role. Finally, since most cohorts were from Asia, the results may not generalize well, calling for replication in African, European, and Latino populations. Implications and future directions Despite these limitations, our findings carry important implications for clinical practice and public health. METS-IR stands out as an easy-to-use biomarker for assessing CVD risk in adults without symptoms, outperforming some traditional IR measures because it draws on standard lab values ( 7 ). With HRs like 1.65 for composite CVD, 1.82 for CAD, and 1.47 for stroke (comparing highest to lowest categories), it could help spot high-risk individuals early, especially those with hypertension or other metabolic issues—and steer them toward lifestyle tweaks or medications to stay below key inflection points ( 11 , 32 , 45 ). On a broader scale, its simple, low-cost nature makes it ideal for widespread screening in areas where advanced tests aren’t feasible ( 7 , 12 , 46 , 47 ), fitting well with worldwide efforts to prevent CVD through better metabolic control ( 10 , 48 , 49 ). To build on this, future studies should test these associations in more diverse groups, such as non-Asian ethnicities or younger adults, to improve generalizability and refine the inflection points. We also need mechanistic research to unpack the nonlinear patterns—for CAD, stroke, and composite CVD—by examining how METS-IR’s elements (like BMI, fasting blood glucose, and TG/HDL-C) interact with factors such as endothelial dysfunction or inflammation. Head-to-head comparisons with other surrogates, like the TyG index, could reveal if METS-IR adds unique value in combined models. Finally, long-term trials that lower METS-IR through diet or exercise would help establish causality and quantify how much risk can be reduced. Conclusion In summary, this meta-analysis demonstrates that higher METS-IR is significantly associated with increased risks of composite CVD, CAD, and stroke, with nonlinear dose-response relationships for CAD, marginal nonlinear dose-response relationships for stroke, and a potential nonlinear dose-response relationship for composite CVD, including critical inflection points beyond which risk accelerates. These findings validate METS-IR as a valuable tool for cardiovascular risk assessment and provide practical thresholds for clinical practice. Despite limitations, the consistency of results across large, well-designed cohort studies supports the utility of METS-IR in guiding preventive strategies for cardiovascular disease. documents.title: Prognostic implications of stress test-induced arrhythmias: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The significance of stress-test induced arrhythmias has been examined in prior studies, but there is no clear consensus regarding its significance.
OBJECTIVES: To determine the significance of stress test-induced arrhythmias.
METHODS: Relevant studies examining arrhythmia in both exercise and pharmacological stress testing were searched for in PubMed, Embase and Cochrane databases from inception to 14 June 2023. The primary outcomes of interest were mortality in ventricular and atrial arrhythmias, and later diagnosis of cardiac disease in atrial arrhythmias.
RESULTS: The presence of any ventricular arrhythmia during stress testing was significantly associated with mortality at all time points: OR 2.11 (95% CI 1.75, 2.54), p<0.00001. This association was still seen in the subgroup of healthy, asymptomatic patients: OR 2.22 (95% CI 1.45, 3.41), p=0.0003. Frequent premature ventricular complexes (PVCs) were associated with higher mortality compared with infrequent PVCs: OR 1.85 (95% CI 1.27, 2.69), p=0.001. The presence of atrial fibrillation (AF) during stress testing was not associated with mortality at all time points: OR 1.53 (95% CI 0.05, 50.19), p=0.81. However, it was associated with later diagnosis of AF: OR 4.60 (95% CI 1.59, 13.26), p=0.005. The presence of atrial arrhythmias during stress testing at all time points was also associated with later diagnosis of coronary artery disease or myocardial infarction: OR 1.82 (95% CI 1.09, 3.03), p=0.02.
CONCLUSIONS: Patients experiencing ventricular arrhythmia during stress testing face double the odds of mortality compared with those without such arrhythmias. Atrial arrhythmia during stress testing, on the other hand, shows no association with mortality. However, it is linked to subsequent diagnosis of AF, coronary artery disease and myocardial infarction.

Atrial arrhythmia during stress testing, on the other hand, shows no association with mortality. However, it is linked to subsequent diagnosis of AF, coronary artery disease and myocardial infarction.

WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC A prior meta-analysis conducted in 2017 found a link between exercise-induced premature ventricular complexes (EI-PVC) and elevated long-term risk of all-cause death or cardiovascular events. WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS Incorporating more recent studies, this paper further shows the connection between ventricular arrhythmias and mortality. It also examines atrial arrhythmias in stress-testing and demonstrates that they are not associated with mortality. This study also highlights the heterogeneity in the definition of exercise-induced PVCs. HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY A universal definition of EI-PVCs should be pursued by major cardiovascular organisations to better standardise and reduce heterogeneity in future studies. Those with EI-PVCs, especially those in recovery, should be referred for further workup including assessment and modification of risk factors of cardiac disease including hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, diabetes, obesity, chronic kidney disease and smoking. As parasympathetic dysfunction is a suspected cause of EI-PVCs, studies evaluating the role of beta-blockade in those with EI-PVCs in reducing mortality in those without established cardiac disease would be of interest, in addition to long-term follow-up of these patients to see if they later develop cardiac disease. Introduction Stress testing is a non-invasive diagnostic method to screen for coronary artery disease (CAD), employing exercise and pharmacological stressors. 1 2 While arrhythmias may develop during stress testing, their clinical relevance remains uncertain. 3 A meta-analysis conducted in 2017 found a link between exercise-induced premature ventricular complexes (EI-PVC) and elevated long-term risk of all-cause death or cardiovascular events. 4 However, the significance of arrhythmias during stress testing has not been thoroughly investigated in previous studies. This paper seeks to investigate the clinical implications of both ventricular and atrial arrhythmias encountered during stress tests. Methods This systematic review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis statement. Search strategy Relevant studies published in English were searched for in PubMed, Embase and Cochrane databases from inception to 14 June 2023. The search strategy for PubMed was: (“Ventricular Premature Complexes” (Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) Terms) OR “arrhythmias, cardiac”(MeSH Terms) OR “atrial premature complexes” (MeSH Terms) OR “tachycardia, ventricular” (MeSH Terms) OR “tachycardia, supraventricular” (MeSH Terms)) AND (“echocardiography, stress” (MeSH Terms) OR “Exercise Test” (MeSH Terms) OR “myocardial perfusion imaging” (MeSH Terms)) AND (“mortality” (All Fields) OR “prognosis” (All Fields) OR “outcome” (All Fields) OR “significance” (All Fields)). The search strategy for Embase was: (1) ‘heart arrhythmia’/exp OR ‘heart ventricle extrasystole’/exp OR ‘supraventricular premature beat’/exp OR ‘heart ventricle tachycardia’/exp OR ‘atrial fibrillation’/exp OR ‘heart atrium flutter’/exp OR ‘supraventricular tachycardia’/exp; (2) ‘stress echocardiography’/exp OR ‘exercise test’/exp OR ‘heart muscle perfusion’/exp; (3): ‘stress echocardiography’/exp OR ‘exercise test’/exp OR ‘heart muscle perfusion’/exp; (4) #1 AND #2 AND #3. The search strategy for the Cochrane database was: (1) MeSH descriptor (Ventricular Premature Complexes); (2) MeSH descriptor: (Arrhythmias, Cardiac); (3) MeSH descriptor: (Atrial Premature Complexes); (4) MeSH descriptor: (Tachycardia, Ventricular); (5) MeSH descriptor (Atrial fibrillation); (6) MeSH descriptor: (Atrial Flutter); (7) MeSH descriptor (Tachycardia, Supraventricular); (8) MeSH descriptor: (Exercise test); (9) MeSH descriptor: (Echocardiography, Stress). (10) MeSH descriptor: (Myocardial Perfusion Imaging); (11) prognosis OR mortality OR significance; (12) #1 OR #2 OR #3 OR #4 OR #5 OR #6 OR #7; 13: #12 AND (#8 OR #9 OR #10) AND (#11). Study selection, inclusion and exclusion criteria The inclusion criteria were: (1) cohort or randomised controlled trials (RCT) comparing outcomes in those with arrhythmia induced by stress testing to those without any arrhythmia induced; (2) study population of adults (aged ≥18 years) who underwent stress testing with ECG monitoring; (3) arrhythmia of interest documented during stress testing: premature atrial complex (PAC), PVC, ventricular tachycardia (VT), non-sustained ventricular tachycardia (NSVT), atrial fibrillation (AF), atrial flutter, supraventricular tachycardia (SVT). The exclusion criteria were the following: (1) no disclosure of any of the primary outcomes of interest: mortality in ventricular arrhythmia; major adverse cardiac events in atrial arrhythmia; (2) studies targeting a specific congenital or acquired infectious structural cardiac disease; (3) studies focusing on patients with a prior diagnosis of arrhythmia of interest; (4) no control group; (5) no arrhythmia of interest; (6) population <18 years of age; (7) abstract only. Two independent reviewers (PYL, JB) screened citations in three rounds. The first round of sifting removed duplicate articles via the citation software EndNote. During the second round of sifting, irrelevant papers were removed based on title and abstract. In the third round of sifting, papers were removed in accordance with the exclusion criteria described. A third reviewer (HY) examined all available texts that passed the three rounds of sifting to confirm that they met the inclusion criteria and documented the final studies for analysis. Data abstraction, risk of bias, quality assessment The data were then extracted independently into a secure, online spreadsheet by two reviewers (SP, RT-M) with another reviewer (PYL or JB) available for adjudication for discrepancies. Two reviewers (SP, RT-M) examined each study to assess the risk of bias and documented it onto a secure online spreadsheet using the Newcastle Ottawa Quality Assessment of cohort studies, 5 with discrepancies resolved with another reviewer (PYL). Outcomes of interest and definitions The primary outcomes of interest were mortality at all time points in the ventricular arrhythmia analysis, and later diagnosis of cardiac disease in the atrial arrhythmia analysis. Either cardiac or all-cause mortality was used in our analysis; if both cardiac and all-cause mortality were provided by the study, cardiac mortality was used. If the study provided both high-grade (NSVT or VT/ventricular fibrillation (VF)) and low-grade (PVCs) ventricular arrhythmia in addition to a control group, the high and low-grade groups were pooled together for the main analysis to avoid double-counting of controls. Frequent and infrequent PVCs are also pooled together if there was also a control group without PVCs; otherwise, infrequent PVCs were used as the control. Arrhythmia during the recovery and exercise phases of the stress test were pooled together if both were available for the main analysis. However, if unable to be pooled together, both groups were used in our analysis separately. To account for the double-counting of patients in the control groups in this scenario, the recovery group would be toggled off in the main analysis by default. If arrhythmia were reported prior to the exercise phase, it was not pooled in the analysis. Data synthesis and analysis The relevant data for the outcomes of interest were pooled and analysed with ReviewManager, V.5.4.1 (Copenhagen: The Nordic Cochrane Centre, The Cochrane Collaboration, 2020). Differences between treatment groups for categorical values were reported as ORs with 95% CIs using a Mantel-Haenszel random-effects model. Heterogeneity of treatment effect was estimated by the Cochrane Q test with p<0.1 considered as significant. The presence and extent of heterogeneity between trials was quantified by the χ 2 and I 2 values, respectively. Publication bias was assessed by a funnel plot using mortality as the endpoint, with OR plotted against the SE of log (OR). The model was toggled temporarily to fixed effects to get the 95% CI line on the funnel plot on the ReviewManager software. All tests were two-tailed and a p value<0.05 was considered significant. Sensitivity analysis Sensitivity analysis for all outcomes was performed by toggling to the fixed-effects model, switching effect measures and excluding each study individually to evaluate the robustness of the outcomes of interest. Any studies deemed poor quality via Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) standards were excluded simultaneously as a part of sensitivity analysis. Two studies markedly to the right of the 95% CI line in the funnel plot were also excluded simultaneously as a part of sensitivity analysis. Results Study selection and exclusion In total, there were 4140 studies extracted for review. After three rounds of sifting, 34 studies were included in our final analysis ( figure 1 ). Of these studies, 29 studies examined ventricular arrhythmias provoked via stress testing. 6 , 34 Five studies examined atrial arrhythmias. 35 , 39 Study details are described in online supplemental table 1 . Figure 1 Sifting process. One of the studies also included a double-blind crossover study with amiodarone; this data was not used. 11 Some of the studies had mortality data of those with exercise PVCs and also in recovery, both of which were included in our analysis separately as combined data was not available. 14 19 27 One study only included mortality data for patients who were medically treated, which was pooled in our analysis. 31 Another study included mortality data for various frequencies and types of ventricular arrhythmia; data for PVCs≥3/hours was used. 32 One study focused only on ventricular ectopy with right bundle branch block morphology. 8 Another study compared different morphologies of ventricular arrhythmia. 15 One study compared complex ventricular arrhythmia with simple, but also had a pooled group with a control group which was used in our analysis. 10 One of the studies also pooled PVCs at rest with exercise and recovery PVCs in their analysis; this study compared mortality with positive and negative treadmill tests; however, in the control group, it only provided mortality for those without positive treadmill tests. 30 One of the studies provided mortality data in the arrhythmia group and total population; mortality for the control group had to be calculated by subtracting exercise mortality from total mortality. 33 One study only provided full mortality data for those who had CAD. 9 Notable exclusions On further review, several studies were removed from the final analysis ( figure 1 ). One study consisted of a population with documented history of VT/VF. 40 Several studies were excluded due to lack of the primary outcomes of interest 41 , 43 or unclear outcome data. 44 One was in abstract form. 45 One of the studies used an electrophysiological study rather than a stress test and was excluded from the analysis. 46 Three were excluded due to not having arrhythmia-free cohorts. 47 , 49 One study studied arrhythmia in athletes with an exclusion criterion of age >35 years of age. This study included patients under the age of 18, and therefore was excluded in our analysis. 50 Risk of bias of included studies The risk of bias assessment of the studies analysing ventricular arrhythmias is documented in online supplemental table 2 . There were several studies that were rated as poor 10 , 1216 18 24 30 ; these were later excluded simultaneously as part of sensitivity analysis. The funnel plot shows that using ventricular arrhythmia mortality outcome was symmetrical but noted to have two studies markedly outside the 95% CI favouring our outcome (increased mortality in the arrhythmia group) ( figure 2 ). These two studies were later excluded simultaneously as part of the sensitivity analysis. 26 30 Figure 2 Funnel plot with ventricular mortality as endpoint. Pooled sample size, demographics Our pooled analysis contained a total of 11 918 patients in the pooled ventricular arrhythmia cohort and 76 436 patients in the pooled control group. Three studies 14 19 27 did not combine exercise/recovery data and therefore used patients from one group as a control against the other group. By default, we used the exercise groups in these three studies and excluded the recovery groups to avoid double-counting of patients. Baseline characteristics of patients are in online supplemental table 3 . Notably, a large majority of patients in this analysis were male. Three studies exclusively studied only men. 7 19 34 Four studies exclusively included patients who recently had myocardial infarction (MI). 10 16 18 32 Three studies analysed exclusively heart failure patients. 11 25 26 One study analysed patients who recently had a cardiac catheterisation; mortality data was only given for those with CAD. 9 Four studies examined asymptomatic, healthy patients. 19 21 23 27 The post-MI, heart failure patients, and healthy patients were compared in a subgroup analysis. Five studies excluded patients with various degrees of resting ventricular ectopy from their analysis. 17 19 23 27 29 One study included resting but non-frequent PVCs; they only noted EI-PVCs if NSVT/VT occurred or if PVCs became frequent. 34 Three studies reported resting PVCs in some patients, but these made up a small minority of patients (<5%). 7 14 33 The atrial arrhythmia analysis consisted of a total of 1999 patients with atrial arrhythmia and 10 670 in the control group. Most of the patients were male ( online supplemental table 3 ). One of the studies evaluated asymptomatic, healthy patients. 38 All studies excluded patients with either a documented history of AF or AF present on resting ECG. Definitions of arrhythmia The studies examining ventricular arrhythmias primarily looked at PVCs, NSVT and VT. Most studies did not explicitly define the PVC cut-off to be considered. Some studies used a PVC frequency above a certain cut-off, such as 10% of all depolarisations during any 30 s ECG recording, 7 34 ≥5 PVC/min, 18 >7 PVC/min, 29 ≥7 PVC/min 17 25 or >10 PVC/min. 24 27 One study documented various frequencies of PVC burden. 32 Other studies used cut-offs such as ventricular couplets alone or in addition to the previously mentioned criteria. 15 16 24 25 Several studies did not include PVCs in their analysis, opting for NSVT or higher-grade arrhythmia, generally defined as three or more consecutive PVCs. 11 , 1333 One study only looked at NSVT, defined as three or more consecutive PVCs but <30 s. 21 One study excluded NSVT/VT and only included PVCs. 6 Three studies compared mortality in frequent versus infrequent PVCs; this data was later pooled in a subgroup analysis. 14 19 23 Two studies used a threshold of PVCs composing 10% of all ventricular depolarisations in any 30 s ECG recording or a run of consecutive PVCs as frequent ectopy. 14 19 One study reported that very few patients would have met the >10% criteria and instead defined frequent PVCs as those above the median average PVC burden of their study population. 23 Most studies examining ventricular arrhythmias did not specify when during the test they considered PVCs but likely included both recovery and exercise phases. Some studies evaluated arrhythmia in the recovery phase of the stress test only. 20 25 Several studies stratified arrhythmia by recovery and exercise phases. 14 17 19 22 27 Some studies examining atrial arrhythmias did not define the arrhythmia. One study reported PAC at a frequency of >5 PAC at any stage based on receiver operator characteristic curve analysis, 37 while another did not mention a frequency of PAC. 39 One study defined SVT at ≥3 consecutive supraventricular beats >100 bpm. 38 Two studies evaluated AF but did not specify the definition nor length of AF in the definition. 35 36 However, one of these studies reported that 81% of subjects with AF during testing had episodes lasting >15 min. 35 All but one study using exercise stress testing did not explicitly mention which phase of testing was used 35 38 39 ; presumably all phases were used. One study did report using arrhythmia at any stage of exercise testing. 37 Stress test protocol Most of the studies analysing ventricular arrhythmias used exercise stress testing, with a few using dobutamine stress testing. 12 13 Of the studies studying atrial arrhythmias, all used exercise stress testing except for one study which used dobutamine stress testing. 35 Indications for stress testing varied among studies. Most were presumably for standard indications of stress testing: evaluation for cardiac disease, with a few exceptions involving healthy patients or patients who have experienced an MI as described previously ( online supplemental table 1 ). Outcome definition All the studies examining ventricular arrhythmia in this analysis included mortality data. Some studies reported exclusively all-cause mortality only, 69 , 13 15 17 21 others reported exclusive cardiac mortality, 7 18 20 24 26 30 32 33 or both. 8 14 16 19 27 28 The time frame of mortality data differed among studies. Follow-up of participants ranged from mean/median of 1 year 16 32 to as long as 20.2 years 27 and 23 years. 19 Most studies had follow-up data ranging from a median/mean of 2–5 years. 8 , 1522 24 25 28 Not all studies examining atrial arrhythmias in this analysis included mortality data. Mortality data were provided in two studies; but one of the studies had subgroups for the different arrhythmias which were all used separately. 36 The time frame for mortality data ranged from 121 days 37 to a mean of 6 years. 34 Three studies disclosed later diagnosis of AF as an outcome. 37 , 39 Three studies disclosed later diagnosis of CAD or MI as outcomes. 35 , 37 One study mentioned that there was no significant difference in cardiac mortality, syncope, angina or non-fatal MI between the control and SVT group but did not report the numbers. 38 Mortality data in ventricular arrhythmia, sensitivity analysis, heterogeneity The presence of any ventricular arrhythmia during stress testing was significantly associated with mortality at all time points: OR 2.11 (95% CI 1.75, 2.54), p<0.00001 ( figure 3 ). There was significant heterogeneity associated with this result: I 2 =80%, (p<0.00001). Excluding any of the studies individually did not affect the result, nor meaningfully reduce heterogeneity. Sensitivity analysis by excluding all studies rated as low quality by AHRQ standards did not change the outcome (p<0.00001). Toggling the model to fixed effect and/or using risk ratios did not change the outcome. Simultaneous exclusion of the two studies that were markedly past the 95% CI line favouring our outcome on the funnel plot did not change the outcome (p<0.0001), but was noted to decrease the heterogeneity to I 2 of 66%. 26 30 Figure 3 Mortality in ventricular arrhythmia with subgroup analysis. Subgroup analysis stratifying mortality by cardiac versus all-cause mortality, indication of stress testing, or grade of arrhythmia did not change the outcome nor significantly reduce heterogeneity. Notably, the subgroup consisting of asymptomatic, healthy individuals still showed an association between mortality and EI-PVC ( figure 3 ). However, the heart failure and post-MI subgroups were not significantly associated with mortality ( figure 3 ). Simultaneous exclusion of the two studies that were markedly past the 95% CI line favouring our outcome on the funnel plot did not change any outcomes. 26 30 Subgroup analysis analysing grade of ventricular arrhythmia failed to show any difference in mortality. Three studies compared mortality in frequent versus infrequent PVCs; frequent PVCs were associated with mortality (p=0.001) ( figure 4 ). Recovery-only PVCs were significantly associated with mortality compared with exercise-only associated PVCs: OR 1.66 (95% CI 1.20, 2.28) (p=0.002) ( figure 5 ). Figure 4 Mortality in frequent versus infrequent ventricular arrhythmia. Figure 5 Mortality in exercise-only versus recovery-only premature ventricular complexes. Mortality data in atrial arrhythmia AF was not associated with mortality: OR 1.53 (95% CI 0.05, 50.19), p=0.81. There was not enough data to pool for the PAC and SVT subgroups, as only one study investigated mortality for these arrhythmias, which found that the presence of PAC and SVT was not associated with mortality. 36 One study combined cardiac hospitalisations and mortality rate in patients with PAC in stress testing and did not find any significant difference; this was not pooled in the analysis as it included hospitalisations which were not one of our outcomes of interest. 39 Later diagnosis of atrial fibrillation in atrial arrhythmia The presence of atrial arrhythmias during stress testing at all time points, was associated with later diagnosis of AF: OR 4.60 (95% CI 1.59, 13.26), p=0.005 ( figure 6 ). There is significant heterogeneity associated with this outcome, with I 2 =68%. Excluding Younis et al removed all heterogeneity, however, there were only three studies included in this analysis. 39 Figure 6 Later development of atrial fibrillation. Later diagnosis of coronary artery disease or myocardial infarction in atrial arrhythmia The presence of atrial arrhythmias during stress testing at all time points was associated with later diagnosis of CAD or MI: OR 1.82 (95% CI 1.09, 3.03), p=0.02 ( figure 7 ). All atrial arrhythmias in one study were pooled together to avoid double-counting controls, but noted to have no incidence of MI in the SVT group compared with the AF and PAC groups; however, combined there was an increased risk of CAD/MI. 36 One study did not document an exact number of MI but reported no significant difference in incidence in those with stress test-induced SVT compared with controls. 38 Figure 7 Later diagnosis of myocardial infarction/coronary artery disease in atrial arrhythmia. Discussion Ventricular arrhythmia The strength of this analysis lies in the incorporation of a substantial number of studies and the robustness of the outcome, as evidenced by our sensitivity analysis. Despite conflicting results in prior studies, the results of this pooled analysis showed that the presence of ventricular arrhythmias during stress testing is strongly associated with mortality ( figure 3 ), consistent with the conclusion of the prior meta-analysis on this subject. 4 In addition, our analysis found that a higher burden of ventricular arrhythmia was associated with mortality ( figure 4 ). The sympathetic stress state during exercise or dobutamine infusion may be the catalyst for the development of PVCs 51 and may represent patients who are at increased risk of developing ventricular arrhythmia/PVCs in the future. In addition to sympathetic activation, vagal activation is another crucial component of exercise 52 and the development of PVCs may be indicative of an underlying dysfunction of the parasympathetic system. Studies have shown that an abnormal balance between both systems can promote cardiac disease. 53 Those who are susceptible to PVCs and other VTs may be at increased risk of mortality either through increased risk of CAD/MI, fatal arrhythmia and/or heart failure/cardiomyopathy. Also, EI-PVC may potentially be provoked from subclinical structural disease; the increase in mortality could be the result of the progression of structural disease. Our subgroup analysis demonstrated increased mortality regardless of whether the stress test was done in asymptomatic, healthy patients compared with those who were being evaluated for cardiac disease. Interestingly, this was not seen in our heart failure and post-MI subgroups, although there was a trend towards increased mortality ( figure 3 ). Perhaps this could be attributed to the use of beta-blockers for both established heart failure and CAD that suppress ectopy and later development of fatal arrhythmia and progression to cardiomyopathy. Our pooled analysis showed that recovery-PVCs were associated with mortality compared with exercise-PVCs in the studies that compared mortality ( figure 5 ). 17 22 27 Two other studies made this comparison but were not included as they appeared to include PVCs in the exercise phase with those in the recovery phase, and vice versa when comparing mortality rates. However, they concluded that recovery PVCs were associated with mortality. 14 19 As mentioned previously, parasympathetic dysfunction during and after exercise may be the underlying reason; this is supported by prior studies that have shown that abnormal heart rate recovery after exercise predicted death. 54 55 Significant heterogeneity was found in the analysis of ventricular arrhythmia. One plausible explanation is the large number of studies using different populations and comorbidities that are bound to introduce heterogeneity; also, some of the studies included specific subsets of patients, such as post-MI ( figure 3 ). However, the pooled analysis that evaluated healthy, asymptomatic patients still showed this association was statistically significant (p=0.0003), suggesting this is an association that cannot solely be explained by comorbid cardiac conditions. Other plausible sources of heterogeneity include the different time frames at which data was collected and the various definitions at which the studies deemed to be ventricular ectopy. Subgroup analysis did not yield any meaningful change in the heterogeneity. Despite the significant heterogeneity, the direction of effect was consistent among studies, indicative of an overall uniform effect; use of the random effects model also should account for such. Clinicians should be mindful of the link between stress test-induced ventricular arrhythmia and mortality in clinical practice. Closer follow-up may be warranted, even in those who may be otherwise healthy. Atrial arrhythmias Atrial arrhythmias during stress testing do not appear to be associated with mortality but are associated with later diagnosis of AF. It has been shown that frequent PACs are associated with an increased risk of AF 56 and that those with a substrate for AF without clinical disease can develop new-onset AF during sympathetic stress. 57 58 A plausible explanation is that the stress testing triggers arrhythmia in those with this substrate; these patients may be more likely to develop AF in the future. This analysis also showed that atrial arrhythmias during stress testing are associated with later diagnosis of CAD or MI. AF and CAD share similar risk factors 59 and often coexist. Small studies in the past demonstrated that PACs were more common in those with heart disease, 60 61 and one study showed that PACs and SVT were associated with the development of patients with AF with known CAD. 62 Therefore, a plausible explanation for our findings is that subclinical AF can be preceded by PAC/SVT/AF which is unmasked by stress testing; patients may be more likely to have subclinical CAD. Interestingly, atrial arrhythmia was not associated with mortality in our analysis despite increased risk of MI or CAD. Our atrial arrhythmia analysis was limited by a lack of studies; perhaps this pooled analysis did not have enough power to detect a change in mortality. Further studies should examine the relationship between stress test-induced atrial arrhythmia and further cardiac events. Limitations There are several limitations to this study. All the studies were observational studies rather than RCTs, leading to the possibility of publication bias, among other biases inherent to observational studies that may skew the results. Second, there was significant heterogeneity associated with the outcome of mortality in stress test-induced ventricular arrhythmia; however, there appears to be a consistent direction of effect. This effect was still seen in our subgroup of healthy individuals receiving stress testing, suggesting there is an effect independent of comorbid cardiac conditions. As mentioned in the discussion, a possible source is the significant heterogeneity in the definitions of ventricular ectopy in the different studies. Excluding two outliers from the analysis reduced the heterogeneity to I 2 =66%. Third, some studies did not describe baseline medications, including beta blockers and antiarrhythmic medications which could affect the results of the study. Fourth, most studies did not indicate whether those with resting PVCs were excluded from the analysis. Lastly, some studies rated as poor quality by AHRQ standards were included in this analysis in an effort to be inclusive; many of these studies did not control for cardiovascular risk factors ( online supplemental table 2 ). However, sensitivity analysis excluding all of these studies simultaneously did not change the outcome. Conclusions Ventricular arrhythmia during exercise and pharmacological stress testing is associated with mortality. Atrial arrhythmias during stress testing are associated with future development of AF and CAD but not associated with mortality. Future directions A universal definition of EI-PVCs should be pursued by major cardiovascular organisations to better standardise and reduce heterogeneity in future studies. We suggest a definition like that proposed by Partington et al , which denotes EI-PVCs if the frequency increases compared with rest. Clinicians should take note of arrhythmias provoked during stress testing and use it as an opportunity to investigate underlying cardiac conditions. We recommend that those with EI-PVCs, especially those in recovery, be referred for further workup including assessment and modification of risk factors of cardiac disease including hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, diabetes, obesity, chronic kidney disease and smoking. If clinically indicated, further evaluation for structural heart disease and arrhythmia may be pursued. As parasympathetic dysfunction is a suspected cause of EI-PVCs, studies evaluating the role of beta-blockade in those with EI-PVCs in reducing mortality in those without established cardiac disease would be of interest, in addition to long-term follow-up of these patients to see if they later develop cardiac disease. supplementary material online supplemental file 1 10.1136/openhrt-2024-003133 Footnotes Funding: The authors have not declared a specific grant for this research from any funding agency in the public, commercial or not-for-profit sectors. documents.title: Efficacy of Drug-Coated Balloon versus Drug-Eluting Stent for Patients with De Novo Coronary Artery Disease: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
documents.abstract:
Objectives: This meta-analysis compared the efficacy and safety of drug-coated balloon (DCB) angioplasty with drug-eluting stent (DES) for the treatment of de novo coronary artery disease.
METHODS: Following PRISMA guidelines, we conducted a systematic search of major databases, including Cochrane, Medline, Embase and ClinicalTrials.gov, to identify eligible randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing DCB and DES. Mantel-Haenszel model was used for dichotomous outcomes. Risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using a random-effects model using RevMan software.
RESULTS: Thirteen RCTs with a total of 4,686 patients were included. The analysis found no significant differences between DCB and DES for all-cause mortality (RR: 1.11, 95% CI: 0.81-1.53, p = 0.51) or myocardial infarction (RR: 0.80, 95% CI: 0.56-1.15, p = 0.23). Similarly, no significant differences were observed for cardiac death (RR: 1.33, 95% CI: 0.86-2.05, p = 0.19), target lesion revascularization (RR: 1.19, 95% CI: 0.64-2.21, p = 0.59), or target vessel revascularization (RR: 1.34, 95% CI: 0.79-2.28, p = 0.28).
CONCLUSION: This meta-analysis demonstrates comparable efficacy and safety outcomes for DCBs and DES in the treatment of de novo coronary artery disease. While DCBs offer a viable alternative, particularly for high-risk patients or those unsuitable for prolonged dual antiplatelet therapy, further large-scale studies are warranted to strengthen these findings and refine clinical recommendations. .

Abstract Objectives This meta-analysis compared the efficacy and safety of drug-coated balloon (DCB) angioplasty with drug-eluting stent (DES) for the treatment of de novo coronary artery disease. Methods Following PRISMA guidelines, we conducted a systematic search of major databases, including Cochrane, Medline, Embase and ClinicalTrials.gov, to identify eligible randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing DCB and DES. Mantel-Haenszel model was used for dichotomous outcomes. Risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using a random-effects model using RevMan software. Results Thirteen RCTs with a total of 4,686 patients were included. The analysis found no significant differences between DCB and DES for all-cause mortality (RR: 1.11, 95% CI: 0.81–1.53, p = 0.51 ) or myocardial infarction (RR: 0.80, 95% CI: 0.56–1.15, p = 0.23 ). Similarly, no significant differences were observed for cardiac death (RR: 1.33, 95% CI: 0.86–2.05, p = 0.19 ), target lesion revascularization (RR: 1.19, 95% CI: 0.64–2.21, p = 0.59 ), or target vessel revascularization (RR: 1.34, 95% CI: 0.79–2.28, p = 0.28 ). Conclusion This meta-analysis demonstrates comparable efficacy and safety outcomes for DCBs and DES in the treatment of de novo coronary artery disease. While DCBs offer a viable alternative, particularly for high-risk patients or those unsuitable for prolonged dual antiplatelet therapy, further large-scale studies are warranted to strengthen these findings and refine clinical recommendations. Highlights of the Study Thirteen trials with a total of 4,686 patients were included. Drug-coated balloon and stent were comparable in terms of all-cause mortality and myocardial infarction. Drug-coated balloon and stent were comparable in terms of cardiac death, target lesion revascularization, or target vessel revascularization. Introduction Coronary artery disease (CAD) is a major cause of morbidity and mortality, with nearly 1 in 20 adults aged 20 and older reported to have the disease [ 1 , 2 ]. The disease’s progression often results in reduced blood flow to the heart, manifesting as ischemia, myocardial infarction, or even sudden cardiac death. Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) using drug-eluting stents (DESs) has emerged as the standard treatment for restoring coronary artery patency. DES prevents acute vessel closure [ 1 ] and has been associated with significantly lower rates of stent thrombosis in comparison with a bare metal stent (BMS) [ 2 , 3 ]. However, neointimal atherosclerosis still develops in 1–1.5% of patients [ 4 , 5 ] and long-term dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) is crucial [ 6 , 7 ]. To avoid stent-related complications and the need for longer DAPT, the search for alternative therapy continues [ 8 ]. In this context, drug-coated balloons (DCBs) represent a promising alternative intervention for treating de novo coronary lesions. A single inflation of DCB allows for rapid and homogeneous delivery of antiproliferative drugs into the vessel wall without leaving a foreign body [ 9 , 10 ]. DCBs have also been established as a therapeutic option for in-stent restenosis (ISR) of bare metal stent and DES [ 11 – 13 ]. European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines initially endorsed DCB as a class I recommendation [ 14 ]. However, newer ESC guidelines recommend DES over DCB [ 15 ]. Several meta-analyses have attempted to compare the efficacy and safety of DCB versus DES in de novo CAD [ 16 , 17 ]. However, the recently published REC-CAGEFREE I trial by Gao et al. [ 18 ] is the largest randomized controlled trial (RCT) on this topic, evaluating 2,272 patients. Therefore, an updated systematic review and meta-analysis is warranted. We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis to compare the efficacy and safety of DCB with DES in patients with de novo coronary lesions. Methods We performed this systematic review and meta-analysis in accordance with the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ 19 ]. We reported it according to the PRISMA statement [ 20 ]. Our protocol is registered with PROSPERO (CRD42024629228). Data Searches and Sources We searched the following databases: Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Medline, Embase, and ClinicalTrials.gov from inception to November 2024. MeSH terms and keywords for “Coronary Balloon Angioplasty” and “Drug-Eluting Stent” were used. Reference list of included studies and similar systematic reviews were also screened to identify further relevant studies. Eligibility Criteria All RCTs comparing DCB with DES for de novo coronary lesions were included. All studies other than RCTs such as quasi-randomized, observational studies and trials conducted on animals were excluded. No language or data restrictions were applied. Study Selection and Data Extraction Rayyan was used to remove duplicates and assess the retrieved articles. Two authors (A.U.H and H.M.) independently performed study selection by screening titles and extracts. Full-text screening was then performed to exclude all studies that did not meet our eligibility criteria. Any discrepancies over the selection of studies in the meta-analysis were settled by a third author (M.E.U.R.). The relevant data were entered into a premade Excel spreadsheet which included author name, publication year, country name, sample size, study design, mean age, gender, hypertension, diabetes, smoking, ST-elevation MI, PCI, left ventricular ejection fraction, lesion length, type of DCB used, type of DES used, clinical follow-up (in months), and outcomes. Outcomes The primary outcomes of our study were all-cause mortality and MI. The secondary outcomes were cardiac death, target lesion revascularization (TLR), and target vessel revascularization (TVR). Risk of Bias Assessment The tool used to assess the risk of bias in the selected studies was the revised Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool for Randomized Trials (RoB 2.0) [ 21 ]. This tool assesses bias in the following five domains: (1) bias caused by randomization process, (2) bias due to deviations from intended interventions, (3) bias arising from missing outcome data, (4) bias in the measurement of outcome, and (5) bias in the selection of results. The risk of bias for each included study was assessed by two investigators (M.K.B. and A.N.) working independently. Any disagreements were settled by a third investigator (M.E.U.R.). Data Synthesis All analysis was performed using Review Manager (RevMan) software. Mantel-Haenszel method was used for dichotomous outcomes. Risk ratios (RRs) and corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were extracted. A random-effects model was used to carry out the meta-analysis. Collective estimates were presented as forest plots, and to assess statistical heterogenicity, the Higgins I-square statistic was calculated. Results Search Results The initial literature search yielded a total of 808 articles. Following a thorough screening of titles and abstracts, 268 articles were excluded, along with additional 231 articles based on relevance. Full-text review was undertaken for the remaining 309 articles, of which 296 were excluded for not meeting the eligibility criteria. Ultimately, 13 RCTs were selected for inclusion in this meta-analysis. A detailed overview of the screening process is presented in Figure 1 . Fig. 1. PRISMA flowchart. Study Characteristics This meta-analysis included 13 RCTs, with a total of 4,686 patients, which met the eligibility criteria [ 18 , 22 – 33 ]. Of these, 2,343 patients underwent DCB angioplasty, while the remaining 2,343 patients were treated with DES angioplasty. Five studies were undertaken in China, 2 were from Italy, and 1 each was from Japan, Croatia, Germany, and the Netherlands, along with 2 multinational studies covering 8 countries. The follow-up periods varied between 6 months and 3 years, and the studies were published between 2010 and 2024. Detailed study characteristics are provided in Table 1 . Table 1. Risk of Bias Assessment in Included Studies The quality assessment of the included studies is summarized in supplementary Figure 1 (for all online suppl. material, see https://doi.org/10.1159/000547099 ). Out of 13 studies, three were deemed to have low risk of bias. Five studies were identified as having high risk of bias, primarily due to shortcomings in the randomization process, issues with measuring outcomes, and inappropriate selection of reported results. The remaining 5 studies raised some concerns regarding potential bias. These concerns were linked to problems such as inappropriate randomization, deviations from the intended interventions, missing outcome data, measurement of outcome, and selective reporting of results. Meta-Analysis of Primary Outcomes All-Cause Mortality A total of 8 studies, comprising 4,012 patients (2,007 in DCB group and 2,005 in DES group), were included in the analysis of all-cause mortality. The pooled analysis showed no statistically significant difference in all-cause mortality between the two groups (RR: 1.11, 95% CI: 0.81–1.53, p = 0.51), with no heterogeneity observed across studies ( I 2 = 0%). These results are illustrated in Figure 2 . Fig. 2. Forest plot of all-cause mortality. Myocardial Infarction The analysis of myocardial infarction included nine studies with total of 4,158 patients (2,077 in DCB group and 2,081 in DES group). No significant difference in the risk of myocardial infarction between two groups was observed (RR: 0.80, 95% CI: 0.56–1.15, p = 0.23 ), and no heterogeneity among the studies ( I 2 = 0%). These findings are presented in Figure 3 . Fig. 3. Forest plot of myocardial infarction. Meta-Analysis of Secondary Outcomes Cardiac Death Six studies, comprising 3,770 patients (1,888 in DCB group and 1,882 in DES group), were included in the analysis of cardiac death. The meta-analysis demonstrated no statistically significant difference between the two groups (RR: 1.33, 95% CI: 0.86–2.05, p = 0.19), with no heterogeneity observed ( I 2 = 0%). The results are depicted in online supplementary Figure 2. Target Lesion Revascularization A total of 11 studies, involving 3,812 patients (1,908 in DCB group and 1,904 in DES group), were analyzed for TLR. No significant difference between two groups was observed (RR: 1.19, 95% CI: 0.64–2.21, p = 0.59 ), though moderate heterogeneity was noted ( I 2 = 58%). These findings are illustrated in online supplementary Figure 3. Target Vessel Revascularization The analysis of TVR included seven studies with 3,917 patients (1,962 in the DCB group and 1,955 in the DES group). The pooled results indicated no significant difference between these groups (RR: 1.34, 95% CI: 0.79–2.28, p = 0.28), with substantial heterogeneity observed ( I 2 = 66%). The findings are displayed in online supplementary Figure 4. Discussion Our meta-analysis, which included 13 RCTs with 4,686 participants, found no statistically significant differences in the effectiveness of DCB and DES in terms of all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction, cardiac deaths, TLR, or TVR. Our meta-analysis does not show a significant difference in all-cause mortality between DCB and DES. A review of the literature reveals similar findings in previous studies. Abdelaziz et al. [ 34 ] included 13 studies of 2,644 patients comparing DCB with DES in patients with acute MI. They did not find any significant difference between the two groups in terms of all-cause mortality (OR = 0.88, 95% CI: 0.43 to 1.8, p = 0.73). Murphy et al. [ 16 ] analyzed 4 RCTs, including 1,414 participants that demonstrated all-cause mortality data at 1 year, with no significant difference between DCB and DES in the treatment of small vessel CAD (OR = 1.50; 95% CI: 0.72–3.17, p = 0.28). Furthermore, the results of a meta-analysis by de Liyis et al. [ 35 ] included 6 RCTs with 951 patients. Their findings were also consistent with ours, with no significant difference being reported in terms of deaths between the two groups (OR = 1.57, 95% CI: 0.67, 3.66, p = 0.29). The incidence of all-cause mortality after PCI varies depending on the time frame. One study reported a mortality rate of 4.3% at 30 days and 7.3% at 1 year in consecutive patients [ 36 ]. Another study reported a 30-day all-cause mortality rate of 7.9%, which increased to 11.4% at 1 year [ 37 ]. Understanding cause-specific mortality trends is crucial in effectively reducing long-term mortality in patients with established CAD, regardless of the modality of treatment. Our meta-analysis found no significant difference in the risk of MI between the DCB and DES groups. It is important to highlight that the majority of studies included in this analysis compared DCB and DES predominantly in small vessel disease, with the notable exception of the REC-CAGE Free trial. Interestingly, while the REC-CAGE Free trial reported no significant differences in clinical outcomes between DCB and DES in small vessels, this finding did not hold true for large vessels. This distinction underscores the need for cautious interpretation when generalizing results from small vessel studies to larger vessel disease and highlights the potential variability in DCB performance based on vessel size. Abdelaziz et al. [ 34 ] analysis corroborates our findings and states that there was no significant difference between the two groups (OR = 0.88, 95% CI: 0.34 to 2.29, p = 0.79). Similarly, de Liyis et al. [ 35 ] also state that there were no significant differences based on their analysis (OR = 1.76, 95% CI: 0.79, 3.88, p = 0.16). However, Murphy et al. [ 16 ] found that in 4 RCTs, there was a significant reduction in MI for the DCB arm at 1 year (OR 0.44; 95% CI: 0.2–0.94, p = 0.03). It is important to note that at the 2-year interval, data available for BASKET-SMALL 2 and BELLO trials indicated no significant difference (OR 0.62; 95% CI: 0.33–1.16) between the two groups [ 22 , 29 ]. This difference in findings could be explained by the varying durations of follow-up for the RCTs. Compared to DES, DCB eliminates the need for metallic implants, thereby reducing the incidence of stent thrombosis, ISR, and stent malpositioning. The foreign material in stents also acts as a deterrent to endothelial healing [ 38 ]. These factors might explain the superiority of DCB, as reported by Murphy et al. [ 16 ] at 1-year follow-up, in reducing the risk of MI. Our meta-analysis concluded that in addition to all-cause mortality, deaths due to cardiac causes also indicated no difference between the DCB and DES arms. This is in line with Abdelaziz et al. [ 34 ] findings. They found no significant difference of risk between the two groups (OR = 0.59, 95% CI: 0.22–1.56, p = 0.29). Murphy et al. [ 16 ] further strengthened this observation in their meta-analysis. No cardiac deaths occurred in any arms of the BELLO, RESTORE SVD, or PICCOLETO trials [ 27 , 31 ]. BASKET-SMALL 2 demonstrated events in both arms at 1 year (OR 2.41, 95% CI: 0.84–6.9), 2 years (OR 1.55, 95% CI: 0.66–3.63), and 3 years (OR 1.3, 95% CI: 0.62–2.72); however, no significant differences were found regardless of the duration of follow-up [ 29 ]. Bai et al. [ 39 ] conducted a meta-analysis of 7 RCTs, comprising 1,238 patients undergoing PCI. Although their results favored the DCB group in terms of cardiac mortality, they were not statistically significant (OR = 0.33, 95% CI: 0.10, 1.04, p = 0.06). All of the aforementioned findings from the previous meta-analyses support our observations. The 6.1% occurrence rate of major adverse cardiac events with the latest generation DES highlights that, despite advancements in stent technology, adverse outcomes remain a significant clinical challenge [ 40 ]. To address these potential risks, the medical community has investigated alternative strategies such as DCB that avoids permanent implants. In terms of TLR and TVR, our meta-analysis concludes that no significant difference exists between DCB and DES. However, considerable heterogeneity limits the robustness of these findings. Abdelaziz et al. [ 34 ] analysis also states that there is no significant difference between the two arms for TLR (OR = 0.9, 95% CI: 0.43 to 1.93, p = 0.80). Murphy et al. [ 16 ] did not report a statistically significant difference in the rates of TLR (OR: 1.03, 95% CI: 0.24–4.39, p = 0.96) for RESTORE SVD and BELLO, or in TVR (OR: 0.74, 95% CI: 0.46–1.20, p = 0.23) for BELLO and BASKET-SMALL 2 trials at 2 years. Our findings are further supported by de Liyis et al. [ 35 ] analysis for both TLR (OR 0.74, 95% CI: 0.37, 1.48, p = 0.39) and TVR (OR 0.76, 95% CI = 0.51, 1.12, p = 0.16), indicating no significant difference between DCB and DES groups. There are a few potential advantages that DCB offers over DES. Unlike DES, DCBs do not leave a permanent metallic scaffold in vessels, thereby preserving the vessel’s natural vasomotion and avoiding the long-term risks associated with stent implantation, such as late stent thrombosis and neo-atherosclerosis. Additionally, the use of DCB allows for a shorter duration of DAPT, which is particularly beneficial in patients who are at a high bleeding risk. Furthermore, it is important to acknowledge that incidence of DES ISR is notably higher in challenging settings such as small vessel disease, long lesions, heavily calcified vessels, and in the presence of systemic factors like diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease. Therefore, highlighting these aspects would provide a more balanced and comprehensive discussion of the clinical utility of DCB in contemporary practice. PCI with DES has been highly effective in treating de novo CAD, but challenges such as stent thrombosis and restenosis persist. While DCBs are currently recommended for management of ISR and small vessel disease, previous literature remains inconclusive on their utilization as a substitute to DES for de novo coronary lesions. Unlike DES, DCBs deliver antiproliferative drugs directly to the vessel wall without the need for a permanent implant, reducing the risk of complications such as inflammation, thrombosis, and impaired endothelial function [ 41 ]. Additionally, DCBs are associated with a shorter duration of DAPT compared to DES [ 42 ]. Both DES and DCBs use antiproliferative drugs like paclitaxel and sirolimus to prevent neointimal hyperplasia. Paclitaxel disrupts microtubule assembly, causing cell cycle arrest, while sirolimus inhibits mTOR and PI3K pathways, leading to G1-phase cell cycle arrest [ 43 ]. In patients with diffuse CAD or multivessel disease, DCBs offer benefit by reducing the need for multiple stents [ 44 ]. Importantly, DCB effectiveness is reliant on optimal lesion preparation prior to elution of the medication to vessel wall. Current recommendations for DCB treatment following lesion preparation with balloon angioplasty include TIMI grade 3 flow, residual stenosis of ≤30%, and a fractional flow reserve of ≥0.75 [ 45 , 46 ]. Fractional flow reserve-guided DCB treatment can potentially improve clinical outcomes in patients by reducing the need for bail-out stenting. The standard method of lesion preparation involves the use of a semi-compliant balloon that is 0.5 mm smaller than the reference vessel diameter. Stepwise increase in balloon diameter is advisable, with the next step involving a conventional balloon with a balloon-to-vessel ratio of 0.8–1.0. Ideally, the DCB should extend 2–3 mm beyond the predilated area and should be inflated for at least 30 s at nominal pressure for desirable results [ 47 ]. The effectiveness of DCB as a substitute to DES is an emerging concept and analyses like ours, and further trials can help tailor future treatment modalities based on patient needs. Our meta-analysis had several limitations that must be acknowledged. First, the trials included in our pooled analysis varied in terms of follow-up durations, with longer durations increasing the risk of attrition. Second, a few of our outcomes showed considerable heterogeneity that might be influencing the results and thereby introducing potential bias, likely due to variations in patient and intervention characteristics. Third, all of the studies included in this meta-analysis exclusively utilized paclitaxel-coated balloons. Currently, there are no RCT data available to support the use of sirolimus-coated DCBs in de novo coronary lesions. However, emerging data are anticipated, with the Selution De Novo trial expected to report its findings later this year. Additionally, the ongoing Transform II trial [ 48 ] is directly comparing the MagicTouch Sirolimus-coated balloon against an everolimus-eluting stent, which will provide further insights into the performance of sirolimus-based DCB technology in this setting. These forthcoming studies will be pivotal in defining the role of Sirolimus-coated DCBs in the treatment of de novo CAD. Fourth, lack of patient-level data posed a challenge in individual assessment of risk factors and disease specifications. Fifth, some of the patients in the DCB arm required bail-out stenting which is not an uncommon occurrence with DCB. This could be attributed to high disease burden, vessel anatomy, or lesion complexity. All of these factors could be a source of variation and impact our study outcomes. Sixth, clinical outcomes were not clearly defined by most studies which could account for the heterogeneity seen in several outcomes. Lastly, some of the included trials were open label due to challenges in masking of the assignment groups. Conclusion This meta-analysis concludes that DCB remains non-inferior to DES in the treatment of CAD. However, due to certain limitations these results require further confirmation by means of more robust and targeted clinical trials studying the effectiveness of DCB. So far, it shows great promise as an alternative therapy to DES and future studies could help utilize its potential in achieving desired clinical outcomes. documents.title: Risk factors for abdominal aortic aneurysm in general populations: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) has a high mortality rate after rupture. This study systematically explored the risk factors associated with AAA in the general population using a meta-analytic approach.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: We conducted a systematic search of PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Library databases to identify relevant literature. The search was conducted through May 2025. Factors considered in more than three studies were included in the analysis. Odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were used as effect estimates and all pooled analyses were performed using a random-effects model.
RESULTS: Thirty-four studies reporting 34,551 AAA cases were selected for meta-analysis. Increased risk of AAA was associated with male (OR: 3.78; 95% CI: 2.80-5.10; P < 0.001), current or ever smoking (OR: 3.39; 95% CI: 2.57-4.48; P < 0.001), hypertension (OR: 1.31; 95% CI: 1.21-1.42; P < 0.001), dyslipidemia (OR: 1.33; 95% CI: 1.24-1.43; P < 0.001), coronary artery disease (OR: 1.81; 95% CI: 1.66-1.98; P < 0.001), cerebrovascular disease (OR: 1.32; 95% CI: 1.18-1.48; P < 0.001), peripheral vascular disease (OR: 1.67; 95% CI: 1.47-1.91; P < 0.001), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (OR: 1.58; 95% CI: 1.31-1.90; P < 0.001), renal disease (OR: 1.91; 95% CI: 1.28-2.83; P = 0.001) and family history of AAA (OR: 2.26; 95% CI: 1.58-3.25; P < 0.001). However, diabetes mellitus was associated with a reduced risk of AAA (OR: 0.84; 95% CI: 0.74-0.95; P = 0.007). Furthermore, the risk of AAA was not affected by advanced age, alcohol intake, cancer, being overweight, or physical activity. The association between AAA risk and sex, smoking, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, renal disease, and a family history of AAA differs between Eastern and Western countries.
CONCLUSIONS: We systematically explored the risk factors for AAA. AAA represent a significant public health concern. Thus, early intervention and health education targeting these risk factors are necessary to prevent their occurrence. Registration: INPLASY2023120024.
